interest:
I am interested in AI, machine learning, large language models (LLMs), large
multimodal models (LMMs), foundation models, retrieval-augmented generation,
research agents, and automated scientific discovery methods that can be
useful for astronomy and astrophysics.

Prioritize papers that could help with:
1. JWST imaging/spectroscopy analysis, especially high-redshift galaxies,
   AGN, and little red dots
2. astronomical source classification, anomaly detection, morphology,
   deblending, photometric redshifts, SED fitting, spectral fitting, or
   uncertainty estimation
3. multimodal models that combine images, spectra, catalogs, tables, text, or
   literature
4. LLM agents for literature review, data analysis, coding, scientific
   workflows, or reproducible research
5. methods that could transfer to large survey data from JWST, Roman, Euclid,
   Rubin/LSST, HST, ALMA, or multi-wavelength catalogs

Deprioritize generic NLP, chatbots, robotics, games, social media, medicine,
finance, or benchmark-only papers unless the method clearly transfers to
astronomical research workflows.

papers.title: AutoSupervision: Closing the Feedback Loop in Scientific Workflows with Grounded Revision Verification
papers.authors: Haobo Li , Eunseo Jung , Wenxiao Zhao , Feng Liu , Jiong Wang , Kaiyi Xu , Zijie Guo , Zixin Chen , Ben Fei , Fenghua Ling , Lei Bai
papers.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have enabled AI systems to assist scientific research and peer review. However, an essential capability for reliable AI-assisted scientific workflows remains underexplored: verifying whether reviewer feedback leads to meaningful and evidence-supported manuscript improvements. We introduce AutoSupervision, which evaluates whether scientific manuscript revisions genuinely address reviewer concerns through grounded evidence. AutoSupervision leverages transparent peer-review records as a natural source of supervision, where reviewer comments specify scientific concerns, author responses describe claimed resolutions, and revised manuscripts provide evidence of changes. Given reviewer comments, author responses, and revised manuscripts, models must characterize reviewer concerns, determine whether concerns have been addressed, and identify supporting manuscript evidence. We construct AutoSupervision from 56,000 Nature Communications articles and corresponding review records. Then we conducted experiments on LLMs, the ablation study, and the case study. Our results show that while LLMs perform well in characterizing reviewer concerns, with GPT-5.5 achieving a score of 0.754, evidence-based verification remains the primary bottleneck, with the best-performing model reaching only 0.501.
papers.Reasons for match: The paper directly addresses automated scientific discovery and verification of manuscript revisions, which is highly relevant to research agents and reproducible research. It uses LLMs to verify evidence-based improvements, which could be applied to astronomy literature.
papers.Short digest: This paper addresses the problem of verifying whether reviewer feedback leads to meaningful and evidence-supported manuscript improvements in scientific workflows. The main idea is to use transparent peer-review records as supervision, where models must characterize concerns, determine if they are addressed, and identify supporting evidence. This could matter for astronomy because it enables automated quality control in research workflows, helping agents ensure revisions are grounded. A concrete workflow could be using AutoSupervision to check whether a revised paper on JWST data properly addresses reviewer comments. However, the paper is based on Nature Communications articles, so its transfer to astronomy-specific manuscripts needs validation.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check if the method is domain-agnostic and can be applied to astronomy manuscripts
Look for details on the evidence-based verification bottleneck and how it might be improved
Assess the computational cost of running the model on large-scale review records

papers.title: Rehearse: Stepping Back from the Confidence Cliff in Self-Improving Autoresearch
papers.abstract: Autoresearch improves machine-learning code by proposing changes, running full training jobs, and keeping changes that improve the metric. The efficiency of this loop depends not only on generating ideas, but also on the agent's ability to decide, before spending a training run, whether a proposed modification is likely to work. We study how the reliability of this pre-execution judgment changes over the course of an autoresearch trajectory. In public AutoSOTA logs (Li et al., 2026; Tsinghua FIB Lab, 2026), the fraction of helpful modifications falls from 70% in the first two iterations to 43% by iteration 6+. On 296 same-baseline modification pairs from 39 paper-derived AutoSOTA tasks, each containing one modification that improved the metric and one that did not, with measured outcomes hidden, an LLM judge given candidate rationales but no prior-attempt history reaches 79.5% accuracy on the pairs where strict consensus returns a verdict. On the full 366-pair benchmark, however, this ability weakens substantially late in the loop. As successful changes accumulate, selective accuracy - accuracy conditioned on a strict-consensus verdict - falls from 82.8% to 56.9%, while the judge remains willing to decide. We call this operational pattern the confidence cliff. Rehearse implements the loop change as a lightweight skill for autoresearch loops: propose several ideas, compare them before execution, run the most promising, and judge with a focused memory of similar past attempts and outcomes. This focused outcome memory raises late selective accuracy to 83.5%. Across 4,000 budgeted training runs over three loops, Rehearse improves the endpoint under the same training-run budget on nanochat, image classification, and time-series forecasting.
papers.Reasons for match: The paper directly addresses self-improving autoresearch loops, which are highly relevant to automated scientific discovery and research agents for astronomy.
papers.Short digest: This paper studies the reliability of pre-execution judgment in autoresearch loops, where an agent proposes code changes and runs training jobs. The main finding is that the agent's ability to predict whether a modification will help declines over iterations, a 'confidence cliff'. The proposed Rehearse skill improves late selective accuracy by using focused memory of past attempts. This matters for astronomy because it could improve the efficiency of automated pipelines that iteratively improve data analysis code. The workflow would be to apply Rehearse to an autoresearch loop that optimizes photometric redshift estimation or source classification. The limitation is that it requires a training-run budget and a well-defined metric to optimize.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check if the method is tested on scientific or astronomical code optimization
Look for details on how the focused memory is implemented and its computational cost

papers.title: FaithEyes: Towards Faithful Tool Use via Multi-Agent Process-Image Verification
papers.authors: Haoqing Wang , Xingrun Xing , Wei Xia , Ziheng Li , Yehui Tang
papers.abstract: Agentic vision-language models (VLMs), which interleave textual reasoning with explicit tool calls such as cropping and code-based image manipulation, have emerged as a compelling paradigm for reliable and interpretable multimodal reasoning. However, recent studies have revealed that such models often use tools unfaithfully. Many process images are irrelevant to the question (e.g., the tool crops the wrong region or misses the queried target), yet the call still receives full credit and the model still answers correctly. Such decorative or misaligned tool calls waste computation and reveal that the model leans on prior knowledge or the original image rather than the evidence it retrieves. This may stem from two limitations of prevailing methods: the tool reward fails to distinguish useful from useless calls, and tool feedback carries no signal of usefulness. To this end, we introduce FaithEyes, a multi-agent self-judging framework. Concretely, we use a VLM to judge whether each process image helps answer the question. The judgement is injected into the reasoning context as part of the tool observation to help subsequent reasoning, and meanwhile is used to scale the tool reward by the helpful-tool ratio to suppress reward hacking. To keep judgement available at evaluation and thus ensure train-test consistency, we further design a multi-agent framework where the model itself serves as a subagent to judge the tool calls from main agent, eliminating any dependence on an external model at inference. Training via a two-stage SFT + RL pipeline on adapted open-source data, FaithEyes attains competitive or superior accuracy across visual perception and reasoning benchmarks, while markedly improving tool faithfulness. The homepage is at this https URL .
papers.Reasons for match: Multi-agent tool-use verification for VLMs is highly relevant to building reliable research agents for astronomy, especially for image analysis.
papers.Short digest: The paper addresses the problem of vision-language models using tools unfaithfully, such as cropping wrong regions. It introduces a multi-agent framework where a subagent judges whether tool outputs help answer the question, improving tool faithfulness. For astronomy, this could be used to build agents that analyze JWST images with cropping or code-based tools, ensuring they use evidence correctly. A workflow might be an agent that crops regions of interest in galaxy images and verifies the crop is relevant before further analysis. The method requires training on adapted data, so check if it can be fine-tuned for astronomical tasks.
Full-text inspection checklist: Look for the tool-use faithfulness metric and how it is measured
Check if the framework can be adapted to astronomical image tools like source extraction or SED fitting
See if the training data includes any scientific or astronomical examples
Evaluate if the multi-agent design adds significant computational overhead

papers.title: EMBL AI Librarian: Life-Sciences Knowledge Layer for AI Agents
papers.authors: Luigi Sigillo , Matteo Silvestri , Francesco Tabaro , Rajat Bhatnagar , Syed Irtaza Mubashar , Matt Jeffryes , Daljit Nijjer , Vittorio Perera , Ola Spjuth , Julio Saez-Rodriguez , Melissa Harrison , Fabio Petroni
papers.subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Information Retrieval (cs.IR); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
papers.abstract: The web is increasingly accessed by AI agents rather than humans. Every agent needs knowledge, especially in the life-sciences, where agentic pipelines are growing fast. Access to the literature is a crucial part of that need, and resources such as Europe PMC, with over 40M indexed records, are widely used to meet it. Yet these resources were not built for AI agents: they take keywords and complex syntax and return whole papers, so every agent must learn the syntax, issue several searches, and read full papers to find the evidence it needs. We introduce EMBL AI Librarian, a knowledge layer that upgrades the Europe PMC interface for AI agents: an agent asks in natural language and receives evidence that answers it. A single LLM orchestrates the whole knowledge retrieval process: it plans complementary subqueries executed by the live Europe PMC search engine, then reads the selected papers and locates the relevant evidence. We evaluate Librarian across four benchmarks: literature synthesis, claim verification, open-domain question answering, and downstream biology tasks such as protocol questions and sequence manipulation. On ScholarQABench, Librarian improves Citation F1 by more than $16$ points over strong recently published baselines. Used as the retrieval layer of an existing claim-verification pipeline, it increases agreement with expert consensus; and on the open-form LitQA2 benchmark, a GPT-5.4 agent scores about $8$ points higher when grounded in Librarian than with web search. Overall, our results show that equipping life-science agents with the Librarian knowledge layer improves performance across a range of tasks. We release our code publicly at this https URL
papers.Reasons for match: This paper presents a knowledge layer for AI agents that retrieves evidence from a large literature database, directly relevant to building research agents for astronomy literature review and evidence extraction.
papers.Short digest: The paper addresses the problem that AI agents struggle to efficiently retrieve specific evidence from large literature databases like Europe PMC, which are designed for keyword searches and full-paper returns. The main idea is a single LLM orchestrating the retrieval process: it plans multiple complementary subqueries, reads selected papers, and extracts relevant evidence to answer natural-language questions. This matters for astronomy because similar literature databases (e.g., ADS) could be upgraded for AI agents to support automated literature review and evidence synthesis. A concrete workflow could be building an agent that answers questions like 'What are the known SED properties of little red dots?' by querying ADS and extracting relevant passages. Before investing time, check whether the method's reliance on Europe PMC's API and full-text access can be adapted to astronomy-specific databases and paywalled content.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check if the method requires full-text access or only abstracts, and whether it can handle paywalled papers.
Look for details on how the LLM plans subqueries and selects evidence, especially any domain-agnostic components.
Evaluate the benchmarks: are any similar to astronomy tasks like claim verification or open-domain QA on scientific literature?

papers.title: MANTA: Multi-Agent Network Topology Adaptation for Self-Evolving Multi-Agent Systems
papers.authors: Mao-xun Huang , Jerry Wang , Yi-Cheng Lai , Zhengxin Zhang , Claire Cardie , Hen-Hsen Huang
papers.abstract: Large language model-based multi-agent systems improve complex problem solving through task decomposition, agent specialization, information exchange, and intermediate validation. However, existing systems typically treat communication topology as a fixed design choice or an offline optimization target. We introduce MANTA, a framework for Multi-Agent Network Topology Adaptation that enables communication structures to self-evolve at inference time. Before execution, MANTA initializes a task-conditioned topology from prior structural experience. During deployment, it monitors collaboration traces and applies bounded structural updates when the current organization becomes insufficient. These updates can modify agent roles, communication links, execution order, information visibility, and validation pathways while preserving the task interface and agent budget. We evaluate MANTA against representative single-agent and multi-agent baselines on five benchmarks spanning information seeking, tool use, planning, workflow execution, and mathematical reasoning. MANTA achieves the highest average score of 74.0, outperforming the strongest baseline by 5.8 percentage points and obtaining the best result on PlanCraft. These results show that inference-time self-improvement can extend to the architecture of collaboration itself.
papers.Reasons for match: The paper directly addresses multi-agent systems with self-evolving communication topologies, which is relevant to building research agents for automated scientific discovery. The concept of adapting agent roles and information flow at inference time could transfer to collaborative astronomy workflows.
papers.Short digest: This paper tackles the problem of fixed communication topologies in LLM-based multi-agent systems, which limits adaptability during complex problem solving. It introduces MANTA, a framework that lets the communication structure self-evolve at inference time by monitoring collaboration traces and applying bounded updates to roles, links, and execution order. This matters for astronomy because research agents analyzing JWST data could benefit from dynamically reorganizing subtasks (e.g., source detection, SED fitting, literature search) based on intermediate results. I could imagine applying MANTA to a multi-agent pipeline for classifying little red dots, where agents for imaging, spectral fitting, and literature review adapt their collaboration based on data complexity. However, the paper's benchmarks are generic (information seeking, planning), so I should check whether the topology updates are interpretable and controllable enough for scientific workflows.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check whether the topology update mechanism is interpretable and can be constrained to preserve scientific validity
Look for details on how task-conditioned topology initialization works and whether it requires domain-specific priors
Examine the computational overhead of monitoring and updating topology during inference
Assess whether the method scales to long-horizon tasks typical of astronomical data analysis
